hints.content:
$\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 1}g(x)$ represents the limit of $g$ as $x$ approaches $1$.

Let's look at the table and see if the $g(x)$-values seem to approach a distinct finite value as the $x$-values approach $1$.

$x$ | $0.9$ | $0.99$ | $0.999$ 
:- | :-: | :-: | :-:  
$g(x)$ | $9.12$ | $9.75$ | $9.98$ 

As the $x$-values *increase towards* $x=1$ (i.e. approach it from the left), the $g(x)$-values seem to approach $10$.

$x$ | $1.001$ | $1.01$ | $1.1$
:- | :-: | :-: | :-: 
$g(x)$ | $7.03$ | $7.14$ | $7.81$

As the $x$-values *decrease towards* $x=1$ (i.e. approach it from the right), the $g(x)$-values seem to approach $7$.
The function doesn't seem to approach the same value from both sides, so the limit doesn't exist.

question.content:
The function $g$ is defined over the real numbers. This table gives a few values of $g$.

$x$ | $0.9$ | $0.99$ | $0.999$ | $1.001$ | $1.01$ | $1.1$
:- | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: 
$g(x)$ | $9.12$ | $9.75$ | $9.98$ | $7.03$ | $7.14$ | $7.81$

**What is a reasonable estimate for $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 1}g(x)$?**
